inline.s:
Manifesting as a princely body, wherever karma calls.
A mind like a lotus, unstained by the dust.
Enthroned in the deep palace, ever turning the Dharma,
That the original person in each be never obscured.
Sent to Layman Yuan

All along this body has been but a guest;
Today, swinging my arms free, I first go home.
Looking back at the red-dust roads where I hurried —
How much better to rest the mind in the white lotus.
Instructions to the Chan Man Minghai

Beneath the cassock, how could this be an ordinary thing?
Not to seek out one's own mind — that is what most deserves grief.
Drifting through kalpas of vast eons down to this day,
This turning back is truly worth discussing well.
Instructions to the Chan Man Xinwu, Nine Years in Seclusion

Shut in, sitting like a withered tree, nine years the term —
Much like the nine years of wall-gazing at Mt. Song.
Even though the snow may pile three feet deep around the waist,
How many know the one phrase that sets the mind at rest?
Instructions to the Practitioner Xingtong

Treading the pestle with a stone at his waist, as at Huangmei;
In the midnight hour, how could he ever open true eyes?
Only trust that from the first there is not a single thing —
Then you will know the bright mirror is no stand at all.
Seeing Off the Chan Man Kewen, Who Goes to Shaolin to Pay Homage to the Patriarch

Before the rock of the severed arm the snow is red still;
Who is fit to inherit the single vein come from the West?
On this journey, if you but obtain the Dharma of pacifying the mind,
You will revive the very spirit of the first patriarch.
Mourning Dharma Master Chaosong

You came at first from Tushita, summoned by the white mallet;
Now that you have gone, you should once more mount the preaching seat.
If we wait for the Compassionate One's next birth in the world,
We know you will take up again your former embryo.
Sent to Rong, Chief Seat

Boats come and go upon the West River without end;
Since we parted, word and letter have fallen wholly silent.
Only the moon above the pine before your bed —
Deep in the night its shadow falls before you still.
Sent to Layman Sun Tunan

Long have I drifted the rivers and lakes with no fixed trace;
Since we parted I have lain among a thousand peaks.
Who knows I have broken through every dream of men?
Only the empty mountain and the still night bell.
Instructions to Shenyu, Whose Courtesy Name Is Yine (Slow of Speech)

The great Way come from the West is beyond words by nature;
Best to trace the true source back through simplicity and silence.
You must press your inquiry to where conditions are forgotten —
Then you will trust the non-dual gate of Vimalakirti.
Sent to the Chan Man Sanbai

When will you carry your staff and bowl across to Donglin,
And enter my room to speak again of the mind that leaves the world?
Do not betray the autumn-night moon over a thousand peaks;
Its clear light shines alone on the deep, deep shadow.
Instructions to the Attendant Guangkai, Who Upholds the Lotus Sutra

Ever since I heard it myself before the kalpa of ink,
Even then a great karmic bond was already formed.
From now on, taking up again these words from many lives,
Each syllable opens the mind, a lotus on the tongue.
Instructions to the Practitioner Haizang, Who Pays Homage to the Lotus Sutra

Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata, the ancient Dharma-body,
Welled forth out of empty space and showed himself to all.
If in the very place you stand there is no birth or death,
Then every dharma, just as it is, is altogether true.
Instructions to Zuo Funian, a Filial Son of Jiangzhou

The Buddha was, through many lives, a man of filial piety;
With a single thought he always served his loving parents.
If you would seek to become a Buddha through the way of filial devotion,
Among the myriad practices none is truer than this thought.
Instructions to the Chan Man Mingming

You came from afar for the Dharma, clear to Mt. Kuang;
How often, dawn and dusk, you knocked at my gate.
If you would ask the true purport of what came from the West —
White clouds drift away, and then drift back again.
Instructions to the Chan Man Minghua, Whose Courtesy Name Is Daoguo (Fruit of the Way)

On a single reed he came from the West, and five petals bloomed;
From that time the seed of the Way has sprouted of itself.
Only water it diligently with the water of wisdom —
The fruit of bodhi will surely not be amiss.
Instructions to Elder Jianyi of Guizong

To shoulder the true Dharma in the ancient groves,
You must use a diamond-hearted resolve to guard it.
When the light shines forth and the whole body appears,
Each thing and every being is a kindred voice.
Instructions to Layman Wang

Father and son, the family has passed down the Chan of Pure Karma;
Once I sought the true teaching amid the miasmic seas.
And now, re-entering this blessed ground of Mt. Kuang,
We meet as though we had never parted at all.
The Chan Man Mochu of Wuyi Came from Afar to Request Instruction; Being Ill, I Did Not Go, and So Gave This

You came from afar for the Dharma, clear to Mt. Kuang,
Gazing after me with earnest care, coming and going again.
Do not say the old monk is too idle to teach the Dharma —
The white clouds will not let anyone out through Pine Pass.

A splendid lotus throne, thronged about by all the heavens,
Only waits for your light to come and open the Dharma feast.
Do not say the Dharma-body has never stirred:
The tongue's root long since has filled the three thousand worlds.
Sent as Instruction to the Chan Man Guanzhi Yun

Bearing a single bowl, you travel far to other lands;
Wherever you go, following conditions, there is the practice ground.
Do not say the dust of toil is no Buddha-work:
From the sea of suffering you launch a ship of compassion.
Instructions to the Chan Man Jingxuan

This very substance, perfect and bright, is the light of prajñā;
At the portals of the six senses it is never hidden away.
If in every thought the unborn appears,
Then wherever it touches, the mind is free — a field of liberation.
Eight Instructions to Chan Practitioners

The single thought before you must be held with care;
Lucid and alone it shines, never clouded over.
Only that one stroke before birth ever came to be —
It has never been permitted that old Hu should know it.

Coming and going through birth and death, long wretched and forlorn,
Never once halting until one awakens to the unborn.
I vow that in this very body I shall win release —
Do not let me turn my head and sink into the dark again.

One nature, perfect and bright, free of the faintest dust —
It was only that we mistook it for something before.
Let a man but cut off the hindrance of afflictions,
And he will naturally see the original person.

Waves surge on the sea of desire, an endless stream —
Who will turn his head back toward the other shore?
You must hoist the light sail high and be gone;
Until you reach the source's end, you will never rest.

Worldly ties are endless, and suffering has no shore;
One thought of turning back, and you are home.
Recognize the true face you have always had —
Then you will know your cassock was not worn in vain.

This mind need not be sought outside;
It rests only in the single thought before you.
Body and world — look at them from the side of emptiness:
They are but a floating bubble on a calm sea.

At the portals of the six senses, the six dusts are many;
Through the whole world, no one can do anything about it.
But if the mind will shine through them, thought after thought,
Then in daily use you will naturally not follow them.
Six Verses on Pure Land Practice

When all conditions are spent, close and distant ties are gone;
How could these old eyes endure the least mote of dust?
Let not the lotus water-clock of the six periods run dry —
Within the flower there is already a body to come.

At first it was craving thought that drew us into Sahā;
From the Pure Land one must surely emerge from the river of love.
If you would have the lotus flower for father and mother,
It all depends on thought after thought seeing Amitābha.

Seeing, hearing, knowing, perceiving — all are the everlasting light;
The lotus in the ground of mind gives off its fragrance unseen.
If the six senses but hold no stain or clinging,
Then everything before your eyes is the West.

Between the brows, a single thread of white-ray light —
Buddhas and living beings are wholly veiled within it.
If only it stays unclouded before you,
The lotus of the mind's ground gives fragrance unseen.

The toil and dust of the five turbidities is fit to be loathed and left;
The Pure Land of the West is the appointed place of return.
Only let thought after thought bring forth the light,
And you will see the flower open in the pool of seven jewels.

The Pure Land was never something to seek outside;
The single thought before you must know how to rest.
Turn and look where deluded thoughts dissolve —
That is the Pure Land's foremost prize.
Great Snow

Ten thousand mountains, ice and snow frozen to the root;
One whole body and mind chilled to the very bone.
Remembering the six years of hunger and want —
It makes a man's nose sting before he knows it.
Reply to Liu Sanwei, Grand Counselor

Clouds and mountains a thousand li away — here is this mind;
Let me send a single word to Donglin.
If you do not betray the lotus covenant,
The White Lotus Society's quiet tryst may still be sought.
Layman Huayu Upholds the Avatamsaka Sutra and Sent His Nephew Juezhi to Request Instruction, So I Send This

The Flower Treasury's adornment is wondrous beyond compare;
Boundless Buddha-lands are a single mote of dust.
If in thought after thought the light appears,
Then you are one who is freed by following conditions.
Instructions to the Novice Zaizhen

On the road of birth and death, suffering lasts the longest;
Best to seek a good remedy from a teacher.
If you can swing your arms and go in peace,
You must bow to the Dharma King in the gate of emptiness.
The Chan Man Yunzhen Came from Wutai to Visit Shuangjing

Old footprints in the Vajra Pit remain;
Since we parted, cloud-mountains have barred us a thousandfold.
Tonight, across the vast sky, snow for a thousand li —
In that year I sealed the cave's mouth fast.
The Dream Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicle Thirty-Nine
Miscellaneous Discourses

The red dust rolls on; the world's road stretches far.
How many heroes have been wholly undone by it!
Delights that please the heart, poetry and wine that make one forget care —
the zither and books are elegant, yet still they yield a step.
Golden Valley and Orchid Pavilion are wastelands now.
Though a hollow name remains, it is gone along with the men.
To meet a monk beneath the bamboos, with no regard for the eyes of others —
is this merely stealing a moment's leisure? It is a mere excuse.
Thus one knows that leaving the world is the highest move of all;
pity that people of the day are blind to it and do not awake.
Amid the five desires, all kinds of evil conditions
are like boiling water and splitting flame.
To bring forth a single thought for the sake of birth and death
is like a lotus growing in fire — exceedingly rare.
If one does not deeply rouse loathing and fear, and seek the way of renunciation,
one can hardly escape being boiled.

Clever people of the world know from birth only worldly fame, wealth, and honor,
and the pleasures of loving wife and children, and think that a human life holds this and no more.
They do not know there is something far greater than this.
The heroes of old who passed straight beyond birth and death had no other means —
they simply saw through this.

What the sages of old knew, they passed on one to another:
deluded thinking has no nature of its own.
If delusion had a nature, then Buddhas and patriarchs would have no way to emerge.
Moment after moment — this is the name of arising and ceasing.
Only one who awakens to the unborn can see the moment.
These words confound everyone in the world.

The samādhi of illusion, the jewel-enlightenment of the diamond king —
in the snap of a finger one transcends the stage beyond learning. So swift is this dharma.
Yangshan dreamed he rose to Tushita Heaven and struck the white mallet;
and the case of Mañjuśrī being banished to the Iron Ring Mountain — are these the same or different?
The World-Honored One deliberately taught the mind-ground Dharma-door in the palace of Mara —
how laughable to say there is no other Pure Land.

All illnesses arise from deluded craving.
When deluded craving is not produced, inverted thinking ceases; this is called nirvāṇa.
All dharmas are unborn — I teach the meaning of the moment.
Arising is itself ceasing. This is not spoken for the foolish.
Can it be spoken to the foolish?

Dream, illusion, bubble, shadow; dew, lightning, the shimmer of heat;
mirror-image, water-moon, mirage-city, plantain.
These ten similes are the foundation for entering the Way.
Those who know them are few.

When the three inches of breath are gone, who is the master?
A hundred years on, what is left behind is an empty name.
The Tathāgata's twenty years of teaching on breaking attachment
has nothing that surpasses this.

Chan Master Zhenxie Liao, in a poem written while sick, said:
Only after illness does one know the body is suffering;
while healthy, one busies oneself mostly for others.
Truly, these are the right words.

The nature is fundamentally neither water nor fire, yet cold and heat arise of themselves.
This is a poem from the days when I lived by the sea, written while ill.
Now, lodging overseas, my old illness has suddenly come on, just as of old.
The illness does not change with the place, nor does feeling shift with circumstance;
yet its savor is quite different — hard to put into words for another.

Su Dongpo said: Whatever one is fond of, one is sure to be blinded by.
Reading his collection from Dan'er, I felt that Juefan, who later came overseas,
visited the old lodging to inquire into his traces, and an old woman answered him:
Master Su could not help his fondness for writing poems.
How could even an old woman know his fondness? Is that not precisely a blind spot?

When Dongpo was first banished and came beyond the ranges, he ate lychees and found them delicious, and so said:
Three hundred lychees a day — no harm in being a man of Lingnan forever.
When I first read this, I thought it mere pretense.
I have lived here nearly six years now; whenever a new season comes round,
I find myself reciting it a hundred times over without knowing it.

All my life I have loved the calligraphy of the Jin and Tang masters, and at times I made a refined pursuit of it;
the four masters of the Song I had not yet taken thought of.
Only when I was banished overseas did I often recall the flavor of Dongpo's thatch hut at Dan'er,
and before I knew it my brushwork drew near to his.
Xianzhi said: Outsiders — how could they ever know of this? These words have a rare savor.
The marvel of calligraphy is truly not easy to speak of.
Those who copied calligraphy in ancient times were many, but none of their words goes to the ultimate.
Only I have said: like a wild goose crossing the long sky, its shadow sinking into autumn water.
This is what the Chan school calls the one phrase that overturns everything to the bottom.
If a student can see through here, he may inquire into the highest vehicle of calligraphy.

When men of old discussed poetry, they always compared it to Chan.
They little knew that poetry is true Chan.
Tao Jingjie wrote: Plucking chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge, I gaze at leisure on the southern hills;
the mountain air is lovely at day's end, and the birds return together.
And at the end: Here there is a true meaning; I would tell it, but have forgotten the words.
Lines such as these, taken as poetry, are like a child reciting the first primer.
Among the Tang, only Li Taibai's words create the wondrous of themselves —
he could speak it without knowing Chan.
As for Wang Wei, whose words are mostly Buddhist,
later men vied in praising his skill in Chan; but was it Chan?
It was only literary Chan, not like Tao and Li, who reached beyond words.

When I was young, I read Prince Chen Si's Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luo:
Graceful as a startled swan, gentle as a sporting dragon.
I took it only as describing the goddess, and often said privately that a startled swan could be seen,
but a sporting dragon I did not know.
Long ago, when I lived by the sea, one early dawn the clouds were red though the sun was not yet up,
and for ten thousand li there was no cloud; sea and sky were one color.
Suddenly I saw a wisp of cloud spring up in the vast void, and the seawater flow backwards into the sky,
as though the Milky Way were hung across the nine heavens. I thought it a great marvel.
Then in a moment I saw a dragon coiling in the clouds, head and horns, scales and shell
as clear as something in the palm of my hand. It fell from the sky into the sea,
and the grace of its coiling was too wondrous for words;
nothing in the world could be compared to it.
Then I knew that the ancients did not speak at random.
Reflecting further, this is not true of dragons alone: the Buddha's benefiting of living beings,
his awe-inspiring deportment fully complete, is therefore called the conduct of a great one — like dragon and elephant, as they say.
Knowing Where to Rest

My teacher, the Buddha, the sage, left home to study the Way and rested at the Snow Mountains to practice;
when he attained perfect enlightenment, he at once took his seat in the field of bodhi and taught the Dharma.
The Snow Mountains are a place of coolness.
His meaning was that living beings share the five desires and are all burned by the fire of affliction,
boiling day and night without cease; and if we alone wish to leave it behind,
unless we place ourselves in a place wholly cut off, burying body and mind
amid ten thousand fathoms of ice and snow, letting the cold pierce to the bone,
freezing and starving there, dying the great death and then coming back to life —
how else could we stop the fierce flames and escape being melted away?
Thus my teacher rested here to practice, in the field of bodhi's enlightenment.
And it is said that this ground is made of diamond, the place of utmost firmness.
What he taught was the Dharma-door of the ocean of nature.
The ocean of wisdom has no nature of its own; deluded, it becomes karma and consciousness,
and so it is called the ocean of storehouse consciousness, moved by the wind of the ever-abiding state.
Awakened, it becomes enlightenment and wisdom, and so it is called the ocean of enlightenment,
whose nature is clear and perfect; perfect and clear, enlightenment is originally wondrous.
The meaning is to show that living beings share this same source of Dharma-nature,
and only deludedly have the distinctions of stillness and movement, delusion and awakening.
He wished to let us, by means of movement, contemplate stillness; by means of delusion, illumine awakening;
not to be toppled by the bewilderments of Mara and outsiders,
not to be moved by the winds of circumstance.
Unless one takes one's stand on the most utterly firm ground,
how else could one crush the heterodox, establish the great work?
Therefore my teacher took his stand here and taught the Dharma.
Seen in this light, the ground my teacher took is the ground he wished us all to take.
Hence my interest in Narayana. Narayana means firm and solid.
It stands facing the great sea, majestic as a Dharma-gate; its dwelling is named Ocean Seal,
bright as samādhi. It is said: In resting, know where to rest.
If we rest here, we may be said to rest where we should rest.
It is also said: To dwell in benevolence is beautiful. If one chooses not to dwell in benevolence, how can one be wise?
And again: The little yellow bird rests on the slope of the hill.
In resting, it knows where to rest — can a human being be less than a bird?
I shall repeat these words three times over.
Contentment in Poverty

It is said: Poor yet not flattering, rich yet not arrogant.
Arrogance loses one's wealth; flattery offers up one's poverty.
Therefore it is better to be poor and happy.
Poor and happy, then nothing is not a joy.
Thus Yan Hui's mean lane, Yuan Xian's bare walls, Zilu's padded gown, Rong Gong's plain belt —
did they rejoice in nothing, and yet rejoice? If one gains this joy,
then even the whole world could not be exchanged for it.
Ah, no wonder Xu You and Wu Guang, Nie Que and Pi Yi
bore the conduct of absolute renunciation.
Confucius also said: With coarse rice to eat, water to drink, and my bent arm for a pillow,
joy is there as well. Wealth and honor gained by unrighteousness are to me as drifting clouds.
The Essentials of Learning
Tending the Mind

Setting the mind at rest lies in emptiness; maintaining the mind lies in evenness;
employing the mind lies in illumination; awakening the mind lies in forgetting.
The substance of the mind is originally empty; when desires cross and mingle,
and deluded thoughts pile up, there is not a single gap left.
Thus the vital breath steams and the body grows dim, flickering and burning, and there is no peace.
Therefore it is said: Clear away things and it is bright and open; if you do not clear them away, it is not empty;
if not empty, not bright; if not bright, not at peace.
Thus setting the mind at rest lies in emptiness.
The mind is originally thusness; within and without are equal.
Its unevenness comes from weighing light and heavy.
Thus the foolish weigh the outer heavy, the wise weigh the inner heavy, the sage forgets both.
He who weighs the outer heavy falls; he who weighs the inner heavy strains;
he who forgets both is even. Even, then nothing is not centered.
Thus maintaining the mind lies in evenness.
The substance of the mind is originally bright and illuminates all;
it is only because of its muddy dimness that there is anything it does not illumine.
Look at people in the world: day by day their muddiness increases,
and even in action they have no means to mirror themselves.
Thus employing the mind lies in illumination.
The mind is originally undeluded; it is deluded because illumination is lost.
When delusion is dispelled, illumination too dissolves.
Thus awakening the mind lies in forgetting.

Contemplating the mind is the first and most subtle of Dharma-doors.
The mind is the master of the whole body and the root of all practices.
If the mind is not clear, those who would have the body upright and conduct correct are few.
Therefore all the various sufferings of the world arise from deluded and inverted thinking.
If inversion is not produced, then arising is itself non-arising.
Non-arising, then though there is arising, there is no arising;
arising without arising, then thought too is without thought.
Without thought, how could inversion arise? If anything arises, it is not correct contemplation.
Correct contemplation is never not correct.
Reading Zhuangzi

The true Lord has no form at all, transcendent beyond the dust of the world.
Then in a flash a single thought goes astray and breaks into this bag of skin —
like a monkey wrapped up tight, ill at ease on every side.
To rise or sit one must be attended; for hunger and thirst one begs to be served.
For fame and profit one busies oneself, selling off fields and gardens.
There is a further kind of folly: one wants one's face admired by others,
powdering and rouging a stinking skin — no different from a specter or a goblin.
Every one of them lives for the sake of others, and so drags down a debt for the next life.
Alas, men ancient and modern — who is willing to be startled by this?
Only the master of Qiyuan had some small understanding of this flavor.
Discourse on the Round Fan

In the summer of the jichou year, having been slandered by a madman,
I lodged in the eastern quarter of Mo. When someone came out with a fan and asked for my writing,
I spoke off the cuff and recorded it.

The great fire sweeps across, melting metal and shriveling stone;
of those who sit idle by a broken window, few escape being boiled by it.
Alas, a human being — if only he takes my skin and bone to sustain himself,
then for food and rest, rising and sleeping, he simply obeys its command.
It makes the joy of coolness spring up at once at his elbow,
and the misery of sweltering heat dissolve from his skin;
the swarming of mosquitoes is waved away and they retreat;
the torment of their stinging is brushed aside and quietly vanishes.
Why then boast of growing wings to ride the cool wind,
or mount the flying clouds and roam the six directions?
How sad! Once a cool breeze comes, it is cast away as refuse;
when frost and dew first rise, it is looked on as so much clutter.
Is this not to act without dominating, to succeed without claiming credit?
How could one speak of such a one together with this?
Discourse on Solitude

To speak of solitude is easy; to walk in it is hard.
And to be inwardly at ease with it is harder still than walking in it.
Even amid the churn of worldly affairs, without debating high or low,
the great men of old, whether they went forth or withdrew, acted openly while their minds remained hidden.
Truly it is hard to judge them by outward traces.
Unless one has eyes that can see beyond and holds a perfect mirror of illumination,
how could one give full measure to their countenance?
Ah, no wonder the madman of Chu sang as he passed Confucius,
and Xu You turned his head away from Yao and Shun.
Yet was it that these two were right and the three sages wrong?
Each affirmed his own as right; and to take one's own as attainment
is at root no more than shadow and echo before the great Way.
One who hates the shadow and joins in the echo is hard put to hear the purport of solitude.
Let the gentleman who faces the Way take his rest here.
Discourse on Sincerity of Mind, Given as Instruction to Tanzhi

If the mind is not sincere, it is not clear. If the nature is not still, it is not settled.
If the essence is not gathered, it is not complete. If the spirit is not concentrated, it does not roam free.
If the will is not single, it is not firm. If the vital breath is not nurtured, it is not harmonious.
If anger is not checked, it is not calmed. If desire is not blocked, it is not made few.
If learning is not discussed, it is not broad. If inquiry is not debated, it does not penetrate.
If the standard is not set, it is not firm. If conduct is not upheld, it is not strong.
Therefore the learning of the gentleman lies in valuing what others make light of,
in increasing what others diminish, in taking what others discard, in gaining what others do not have.
Thus his Way is great and his virtue vast, his person ample and his name honored —
transcendent and without peer.
Discourse on the Marsh and the Mountain

I have heard that Master Zhuang said:
To hide a boat in a ravine, to hide a mountain in a marsh, is called secure.
Yet a strong man can carry them off on his back, and the deluded do not notice.
His meaning is that where there is something hidden, there is something shouldered;
where nothing is hidden, nothing is shouldered.
Yet if one takes no hiding as the highest, I would suggest that to have something hidden
is better than to have nothing hidden.
Therefore it is said: When the mountain cherishes jade, the grass and trees flourish;
when the river stores pearls, its banks do not wither.
Is this not to have something hidden within and something shining without?
Therefore the gentleman values storing his vessel within himself, waiting for the time and only then using it.
Moreover, the mountain's accumulation is thick, and so it is high and all beauties are complete;
the marsh's accumulation is deep, and so it is low and all virtues return to it.
In taking its image from the gentleman, there is further meaning here.
Discourse on Awakening from a Dream

The Phantom Man was just then riding a single leaf and mooring on the shore of the phantom sea.
He was about to dwell in the vast emptiness with the teeming multitudes of the shimmering deep, and rest there.
It happened that Mr. Wandering Drifter came by, and touched him and asked:
Ha, how strange! I see that you cannot be fathomed.
Gazing at your form, it is drifting as a cloud; looking at your countenance, it is chill as ice;
tapping within you, it is wholly empty; drawing near, you are warm;
tracing you out, you are deep and profound; sealed, you seem shut in; floating, you seem to ride.
Comparing you, you seem a man and yet not a man. Where do you dwell, what do you do, that you have come to this?
The Phantom Man had no reply. He only murmured assent, silent and still,
without knowing, without recognizing, without showing, without speaking.
He slept and rested with him, sat and lay, ate and drank, rose and reclined, waking and sleeping,
for ten days without a break. Mr. Drifter's heart blazed and his will melted, and he was about to be wholly transformed along with him.
As Mr. Drifter was about to go, he made a request of the Phantom Man:
I am a man of wind and waves; I beg to borrow boat and oars,
to ride the drifting and reach the other shore as my support. Has the Master no intention of this?
He said: Stay. What words are these? Have you alone never seen a dreamer?
When he sleeps through the long night, he must sink into deep drunken stupor, head reeling,
his essence and spirit muddled and dim, his soul and thoughts shaken with dread;
his body seems to lie dead, his mind seems a specter.
He does not shift from his mat, yet a hundred monsters appear;
no more time passes than a moment, yet a thousand years stretch far away.
When he reaches the dim and desolate, wandering and looking about on all sides,
he may climb to the summit of the boundless, or stand at the edge of the unfathomable;
poisonous dragons before him, fierce rhinos behind;
advancing, he treads on danger; retreating, he is pressed by peril;
entering, there is no crack to slip through; climbing, he seems to fall.
And he will clutch at withered branches and pull on rotten vines,
while a swarm of bees clusters at his eyes and snakes and scorpions bind his feet.
At such a time, though his mind is exhausted and his wits worn out,
he has no way to get out, no art to break free, no one to rescue him;
he calls out, but who is there to be his kin?
How panicked and trembling he is, displaying every manner of form and giving voice to groans!
Even if there were one awake, how could he ever be calmed?
Only when he fiercely shouts and leaps up, and with one awakening comes fully awake,
does he look back on the dream: it seems faint and vague,
yet when he seeks it he cannot find it, and when he would speak of it he cannot reach it.
Then he is sure to share a laugh with the awakened and let it go.
Ah, is this true of the dreamer alone? The whole world is like this.
Let the Master try to take this self-awakening and awaken all the dreamers.
Discourse on Medicine, Presented to the High Scholar Li

In the eighth year of my banishment, in the winter of the guimao year,
I happened to leave Caoxi and beg for food wherever conditions led, west of the Ling River.
It happened that an old man with heavy brows and white beard visited me at my lodging.
Seeing his stature and bearing, majestic, I knew him for a recluse.
I asked his trade, and he said: Medicine.
Thus I knew him for a man of attainment.
Someone said: Men of old said, If one attains, one becomes a good minister;
if one does not attain, one becomes a good physician.
I say it is not so. Rather, one who attains becomes a physician, and one who does not attain becomes a minister.
Why? The office of a minister is to harmonize yin and yang and preserve the primal vital force,
to blend all things and show benevolence to the masses,
to bring the ruler to great peace and set the world in order and quiet.
Such is his duty; yet he does not necessarily fulfill it.
And even if he fulfills it, the merit is not necessarily forgotten.
For he puts himself first and things after, and works for profit while offering loyalty;
and he must outwardly borrow the sovereign's authority and rely on many hands to accomplish his work.
Still more, he labors anxiously in the field of gain and loss, right and wrong, honor and disgrace,
and to the end of his life pursues his task, yet his Way does not necessarily shine.
Day and night he toils, wearying his spirit and scorching his thoughts,
until he wounds his own life and injures his nature, growing old and dying without awakening. Such men are many.
How is that attainment?
The physician is the opposite. His office takes life as its charge,
takes benevolence as its mind, righteousness as its substance, others as itself,
the removal of evil as its task, upright qi as its principle, the classics as its measure, and expedience as its use.
Therefore in his treatment he must bring the mind-lord to calm
and set the four limbs in harmony.
Whenever he meets danger and hardship, he employs the wisdom of solitary decision and holds to a stance of standing alone;
he is not misled by the many mouths, nor does he evade the crowd of evils.
In the many approaches to urgency and leisure, in advancing and withdrawing he suits what is fitting,
taking the great mean as his standard and utmost stillness as his priority.
And when the cure takes effect, he does not reckon the profit nor boast of the merit.
Is this not to act without dominating, to succeed without dwelling on the credit?
Were he not the most accomplished man under heaven, how could he enter into this?
Seen in this light, the merit of forgetting oneself is great; the fame of forgetting profit is high.
Those who do not forget receive open reward and hidden punishment;
those who forget both are slight at first and manifest later.
Thus one may know that he who forgets merit must afterward be great.
Alas, if a man could govern a state with the heart of a good physician,
what state would not be well governed?
If he could manage things with a heart that forgets itself, what thing would not be accepted?
When things are accepted, all is embraced; when the state is governed, all is made good.
This is the sage's accomplishment, the able man's business.
Here the arts differ but the merit is one, the names differ but the reality is the same.
How then should one reckon rank by prominence or obscurity,
or measure divinity by noble and base?
Because the old man's conduct is lofty and his medicine wondrous,
I have therefore discussed the secret of medicine, to append it to the old man's travels,
hoping that the reader will not only know the old man's medicine,
but through medicine advance in the work of a gentleman,
and apply it to the world and the state, so that all may behold the transformation of Xuanyuan Huangdi.
The old man is a man of attainment. Know the old man's mind, and there is nowhere one does not attain.
Discourse on the Hall of This Light

Qu'e is called Crane Creek; it was a place where Master Zibai spread the teaching.
The layman He, with his whole clan, served the Master most reverently.
There was the elder Yunfeng, who in the dinghai year built a hall to enshrine the Three Jewels.
In the bingshen year the Master passed by and inscribed it: This Light.
Twenty years later the Master entered nirvāṇa; a further twelve years passed.
The old man came from beyond the ranges to Shuangjing for the anniversary of the Master's entry into the stupa,
and took the road along the creek. The elders and laymen there, seeing the old man as though seeing the Master,
were overcome with mingled grief and joy, and entertained him with vegetarian fare for several days.
There was the elder's son Maoqian, who had received this light
but had not yet understood what he originally possessed. He bowed and begged for instruction, resolving not to forget it.
The old man gladly told him: This is the Master using this hall as a broad and long tongue.
Indeed, the whole ten directions are the light of eternal quiescence.
All living beings use this light at the portals of the six senses, illumining heaven and earth.
Therefore mountains, rivers, and the great earth; sun, moon, and stars; grasses, mustard seeds, men, and beasts;
scaled and shelled, feathered and furred — none does not appear from within this light.
Thus the hall is this light, and this light is the hall,
containing the ten thousand images, embracing all without exception.
Those who dwell in this hall revere the Three Jewels, bow, recite, and take refuge;
the sound of the qing and the name of the Buddha; even wife and children gathered round,
eating and resting, rising and retiring; through the twelve periods of the day, turning and bowing,
joking and laughing, ridiculing and scolding — every movement and countenance
is nothing but the wondrous function of this light.
Even dreams and inverted thinking are still the play of this light.
If one can with a single thought know the way home,
then this light is truly what our house originally possesses, naturally and freely, not obtained from outside.
Being thus ready-made, how could one be blind to every enjoyment,
and be content to be a person outside the light?
Maoqian, what you truly see in daily use, and your skill in applying it,
does not betray what you originally possess. Not only does the Master's Dharma-body abide forever, speaking the endless Dharma-doors
that fill the ear and pierce the heart — you may even, without leaving the dust of toil,
sit upright in the Pure Land. Why then see this hall apart from the light?
Even this discourse of the old man is much like lighting a lamp under the sun, or adding feet to a painted snake.
Let the scholar take note of it.
Discourse on the Meaning of the Buddha-nature of Insentient Things

While I was recuperating from illness at Mt. Kuang, shut away from all conditions,
Kongyi zi knocked at my gate and asked: I beg for food among men,
and I have heard gentlemen discuss the meaning of Buddha-nature.
Some do not believe that insentient things expound the Dharma;
some say that the Buddha-nature of living beings is portioned out to each,
like foam on the great sea; they do not believe it is perfect and complete.
I beg the Master to resolve my doubt.
I said: How stubborn! This meaning is most profound, hard to understand and hard to enter;
without a seed of superior capacity from former lives, it is not easy to believe.
Even the view they hold was spoken by the Buddha — but it is not the definitive teaching.
If one has not verified and believed the definitive Great Vehicle,
and has not inquired of a clear-eyed teacher, and has not awakened to the purport that all is mind,
then there are few who will not form such an interpretation.
That insentient things expound the Dharma is plainly stated in the teachings.
The Avatamsaka Sutra, in the chapter on the Tathāgata's Appearance, says:
Suppose the gods have a great Dharma drum named Enlightenment.
When the heavenly beings are given to heedlessness, a voice comes forth in empty space, telling them:
You should know that all delights of desire are impermanent, false and inverted,
changed and destroyed in a moment, deceiving only the foolish and making them cling.
Do not be heedless; if you are heedless, you will fall into evil destinies, and regret will not reach you in time.
When the gods hear this, they give rise to great fear, shame, and repentance.
Now is the sound of the heavenly drum a sentient thing? Yet it can expound the Dharma and awaken the gods.
As for the clouds of light, the jeweled terraces, and the jeweled nets, each gives forth a wondrous sound,
reciting verses in praise of the Buddha; and even dust expounds, and lands expound —
whose tongue is this? As for the gods of Light-Sound Heaven, who are wholly without perception, contemplation, or language,
yet from within their light a sound comes forth, and each accomplishes its work —
and is the sound within the light uttered from a mouth?
These are all solid proofs that insentient things expound the Dharma.
Again, in the Chan school: Xiangyan heard a pebble strike bamboo and understood his mind;
Lingyun saw peach blossoms and awakened to the Way.
From the mouth of what good teacher did they enter?
It is also said that the Buddha-nature of living beings is portioned out to each;
this too is spoken in the teachings, but it is a veiled discourse for the inferior capacities of the three vehicles,
not the ultimate and supreme word of the One Vehicle.
For the Avatamsaka Sutra says: I now see everywhere, within every body, the accomplishment of perfect enlightenment.
Vairocana is one Buddha; living beings are not one person.
If the Buddha-nature of living beings were portioned out to each,
then every living being would accomplish a Buddha of his own, and all would become many Buddhas together.
If there is only one Buddha, and it is portioned out to each,
how then does it say that within the bodies of all living beings perfect enlightenment is accomplished?
It also says: How marvelous, how marvelous! All living beings possess the Tathāgata's wisdom and virtue-marks.
Now the Tathāgata's virtue-marks are the whole body of the Dharma-body.
If living beings possess it, how could it be portioned out?
The Third Patriarch said: Perfect, like the vast void, lacking nothing and with nothing to spare.
These words say that every person is one body with the Buddha — not merely that the Buddha is so.
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: All living beings are themselves perfect enlightenment —
not merely that they possess it.
Hence Ānanda said: I and the Tathāgata, in the precious enlightenment of the clear mind, are each complete and perfect.
It is said that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my nature, and my nature in turn is one with the Tathāgata.
One moon universally appears in all waters; the moon in all waters is held by the one moon.
One room, a thousand lamps: light intermingling with light.
Such a perfect and vast Dharma-door — when the two vehicles sat in the assembly, they were as blind and deaf,
and it is no wonder that partial views are startled by these words and do not believe them.
It is a pity that in the conventional truth, most students of the Buddha-Dharma
cultivate only the knowledge and views of mouth and ear, and have no true inquiry or real investigation,
and have not awakened to the vast, perfect, and bright substance. Even what they do see —
they merely recognize the shadow of the clear, alert consciousness and take it for the real thing;
and they further fix on this body of blood and flesh, sealing it off as the mark of self.
In truth they have not opened even one eye, and so give rise to all kinds of discrimination,
taking the provisional teaching as definitive and their own view as ultimate.
Now we need not debate whether insentient things expound the Dharma or not,
or whether the Buddha-nature is portioned out to each or not.
Have you not heard the verse of the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm:
If a person wishes to know the principle of true emptiness,
his mind's true suchness pervades the outside as well.
Sentient and insentient share one substance;
every place is the same true Dharma-realm.
Simply keep this verse stored in your breast,
and at the portals of the six senses in all daily use, wherever you see form or hear sound, seal it with one seal.
In time, growing wholly familiar, within and without will naturally be one;
sentient and insentient will be beaten into a single piece.
One day, suddenly and thoroughly awakened, you will then know
that mountains, rivers, and the great earth all turn the root Dharma-wheel together,
and that scaled and shelled, feathered and furred all manifest the samādhi of the form-body.
Outside the mind there is no dharma; filling the eyes, green mountains.
Only then will you believe that Zhaozhou sometimes took up a single blade of grass
and used it as a sixteen-foot golden body,
and sometimes took a sixteen-foot golden body and used it as a single blade of grass.
An ancient worthy, addressing the assembly, said: Assembly, do you see?
Right now the Buddhas of the ten directions and the patriarchs of all generations
together are emitting light and shaking the earth from the tip of this old monk's whisk.
This is to receive it clearly in the mind, not borrowing from outside.
Why then seek Chang'an inside the Hanyuan Hall?
When Kongyi zi heard this, he was filled with joy and leapt up, bowed, and withdrew.
Discourse on the Four Vows

The four vows are: living beings are boundless, I vow to save them;
afflictions are endless, I vow to cut them off;
Dharma-doors are measureless, I vow to learn them;
the Buddha Way is supreme, I vow to accomplish it.
These four are what we disciples of the Buddha, practicing the bodhisattva path, bring forth.
Yet a bodhisattva is not someone else: he is an ordinary person of great resolve
who, amid the dust of toil, has the will to seek Buddhahood above.
The teachings say: If you would seek the fruit of Buddhahood above,
you must transform living beings below. To transform living beings,
you must first resolve to cut off afflictions. To cut off afflictions,
you must first broadly learn the Dharma-doors.
Thus these four matters come into being together.
Living beings are the counterpart of the Buddha; afflictions are the root of living beings;
the Dharma-doors are the medicine that cures afflictions.
Because living beings are boundless, afflictions are endless;
because afflictions are endless, the Dharma-doors too are measureless.
What is hard to save, one vows to save; what is hard to cut off, one vows to cut off;
what is hard to learn, one vows to learn. When these three are possible,
then the Buddha Way, though supreme, can also be accomplished.
These are called the Four Great Vows. Only one of great resolve can bring forth these great vows;
only one who possesses great vows can establish a great work, set up great merit, and achieve a great name.
All this is great practice supporting the vow — not an empty vow.
These four are not sought from outside; they are sought from oneself alone.
How is this made clear? Because our own mind is originally the Buddha,
and is in nature not two bodies with living beings.
From a single thought of self, the self is established; once the self stands, all that opposes it are others.
Others in turn are another self; many selves gather, and living beings come to be.
What living beings are rooted in is rooted in afflictions. When afflictions cling rigidly, the mark of self grows firmer;
the mark of self firm, others do not perish. When the self perishes, others are not established;
others not established, afflictions are empty.
Thus if the afflictions of my mind are exhausted, then looking back on self and others, they are as flowers in the sky.
If I am a flower in the sky, then to seek living beings is like inviting a sky-flower to bear a sky-fruit;
seek them from one another, and they are wholly ungraspable.
This is what is meant by afflictions exhausted and living beings emptied —
not saving them, yet saving oneself.
Thus they come into being together and are also empty together.
Yet no one in the whole world is without a self. Those who have a self all have it through afflictions;
afflictions are at work, not the true mind.
Now afflictions are emotion. If one would cut off afflictions
and cuts them off with a mind of affliction, that is to borrow the rebel's troops and to furnish the bandit with grain.
To enter emotion with emotion is like throwing fire into fire: it is called growing more.
To seek to cut it off so is impossible.
Hence one cannot but learn the Dharma-doors.
The Dharma-doors are the means of going beyond emotion, the implements for dissolving afflictions;
they are what is called the emptiness-dharma. The emptiness-dharma is the Buddha's mind;
the matters it clarifies are the Buddha's conduct.
The student of the Buddha takes our own mind to embody the Buddha's mind,
and takes the affairs of daily use to emulate the Buddha's conduct.
Thus with the Buddha-mind of one's own mind he learns the Buddha-conduct of one's own mind,
cuts off the afflictions of his own mind, and saves the living beings of his own mind.
Then it is like hot water melting ice, with no further effort needed.
Thus the four vows are indeed hard; but if one seeks them back within,
nothing in one's own mind is not complete, and one need not borrow from outside.
If one knows one need not borrow from outside, then this body before us is a self;
near at hand, the brothers, wives, and servants of one family; far off, the people and creatures of the whole world and state —
all are living beings. Seeking back in the mind in daily use before us,
if one does it with a mind of affliction, then even within one's own body the six openings jostle one another —
how much less could one order the family, govern the state, and pacify the world?
But if with this one thought before you, you work with the emptiness-dharma,
then thought after thought affliction turns into the light of wisdom,
illumining living beings and bringing all alike back to their own nature; then you are one body with the Buddha.
Thus afflictions are emptied and living beings exhausted; living beings exhausted, the Buddha Way is accomplished.
All people are my brothers and sisters, all things my companions, vast and greatly equal.
How could the vows be set up in vain?
Seen in this light, the dharma of leaving the world is accomplished right within the world.
From now on, in all that we do, whether serving the ruler or benefiting the people,
let not a single act or a single step fall outside the Four Great Vows —
then all is the practice of Buddhahood.
How could this be merely handling empty matters and lending them to the ear and eye?
By this I express my aspiration: may there be those who gain something from it.
Discourse on Response and Retribution

The Buddha teaches that all the good and evil causes and their retributions in the world
follow like shadow to form, with not the least discrepancy.
Yet those in the world who do not believe call it empty talk.
As for the sage Confucius's teaching on accepting one's fate, there are those in the world who believe it,
yet they are forever reckoning and calculating; they are pleased only when they seek blessings and prosperities,
and hate to hear of calamity and misfortune. This is confusion indeed.
They little know that death and birth are as night and day, and the three ages of rebirth
are no more than the affairs of yesterday and today.
Let me use a nearby matter as a simile. Suppose one invites guests:
whatever is set out for the feast, refined or coarse, abundant or spare,
is prepared beforehand in every kind, so that when the time comes it is spread out, each item complete.
If anything is a little lacking, it cannot be wholly fine. This is a fixed matter.
In one human life, the length of the principal retribution — one's body and lifespan —
and the dependent retribution of family property and wealth, fame and fortune, poverty and honor, noble and base —
every hair of it was fixed by cultivation in a former life; what one enjoys in this life
comes not from outside, but is entirely self-done and self-received.
Therefore it is said: If you would know the causes of former lives, look at what you receive in this life;
if you would know the fruits of future lives, look at what you do in this life.
People in the world rely on their own intelligence and talent, thinking they can bring about fame and fortune,
little knowing that fame and fortune cannot be brought about by talent and intelligence.
It is because one cultivated them in a former life that in this life they happen to meet with talent and intelligence and so come about.
To be delighted on obtaining them is confusion.
Again, when fame and fortune that I inherently possess are destroyed by others,
one hates the person and deeply resents the affair, little knowing
that the measure of my blessing embraces only this much, and that what destroyed it
was in no way something my portion ought to have had —
or that I owed that person a little and so lost it.
To grieve over this and then resent heaven and blame others, until grievances are knotted and never untied — that is a fault.
Thus one knows that Confucius's accepting one's fate is our Buddha's cause and effect.
If one knows how to accept one's fate, then poverty and wealth, gain and loss,
are all entrusted to what was fixed before, all of it made by oneself;
then failure and success, long life and early death, are all simply as one's fate must be.
If one clearly believes in cause and effect, then all that one enjoys in this life
was cultivated by oneself in a former life; it was never something another could give,
nor something that intelligence and strength could bring about.
Even where talent and intelligence bring it about, it is still what one's own portion inherently has.
Being so, why reckon gain and loss, and weary the mind with anxious thought,
vainly piling up resentment and gratitude in between?
If a wise person firmly believes in the response of cause and effect,
he need not reckon the gains and losses of the past; he need only take what is present in this life,
and use it to plant the field of blessing for the future.
Like a farmer in the world who chooses good soil, plows deep, hoes well, and sows in season:
the autumn harvest is reckoned at tenfold or a hundredfold.
This too is plain and clear — except that the fields sown differ in richness and thinness.
The Buddha teaches that making offerings to the Three Jewels — Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha — is the supreme field;
serving one's parents with filial piety is the field of reverence;
relieving the poor and rescuing the suffering is the field of the mind.
I would wish the wise of the world not to reckon past gains and losses,
but only to plant the field of blessing for the future.
If one can cut back useless and excessive expense,
and the wealth spent on extravagance of body and speech, and plant it in these three fields,
then not only will the splendor of future blessings grow —
in this present life too one will be at peace in body and joyful in mind, the foremost of blessed men.
If one can plant blessings in the three fields, and further give heed to the Buddha-Dharma —
using Buddha-recitation to dissolve deluded thoughts, compassion to turn greed and anger,
gentleness and harmony to transform violence, and the light of humility to break one's own arrogance —
then this is the practice of a bodhisattva of great resolve.
If the layman can truly believe this, he should be called the most supreme and valiant of men.
